graph_edge.evidence_text:
Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.
Atorvastatin helps lower LDL cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') and triglyceride levels, and increases HDL cholesterol ('good cholesterol') levels, to improve your overall lipid profile.
Atorvastatin calcium belongs to a class of medications called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly referred to as statins.
Atrovastatin tablets are taken once daily with or without food.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Atorvastatin FDA-approved uses:
To reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in adults with:
- Multiple risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD), but without established CHD. Use: to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, revascularization procedures, and angina.
- Type 2 diabetes and multiple risk factors for CHD, without established CHD Use: to help reduce the risk of MI and stroke.
- Adults with clinically evident CHD: Use: To reduce the risk of non-fatal MI, fatal and non-fatal stroke, revascularization procedures, hospitalization for congestive heart failure, and angina.
As an adjunct to diet to lower LDL-C:
- Adults with primary hyperlipidemia.
- Adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH).
As an adjunct to other LDL-lowering therapies:
- For adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
As an adjunct to diet for additional lipid disorders in adults:
- Primary dysbetalipoproteinemia.
- Hypertriglyceridemia.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take atrovastatin calcium if you have liver disease or cirrhosis.
Atorvastatin calcium can cause the breakdown of muscle tissue, which can lead to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, or dark urine.
Serious drug interactions can occur when certain medicines are used together with atrovastatin calcium. Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you use now, and any medicine you start or stop using.
Avoid drinking more than 1.2 liters of grapefruit juice each day.
Avoid eating foods that are high in fat or cholesterol. Atrovastatin is often used in conjunction with a cholesterol-lowering diet.

candidate_edges.subject: Atorvastatin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to prevent or lower the risk of the medical event or condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
When cholesterol and fats build up along your artery walls, in a process called atherosclerosis, they narrow the blood vessels and reduce blood and oxygen flow to your heart, brain, and other parts of your body. By slowing cholesterol production, atorvastatin helps prevent this buildup to keep blood flowing more freely to vital organs.
Lowering your blood level of cholesterol and fats with atorvastatin may help prevent heart disease, angina (chest pain), strokes, and heart attacks.
Your healthcare provider will check your blood lipid levels regularly to assess how well your treatment is working. These measurements include:
- LDL-C: Low-density lipoprotein (“bad” cholesterol)
- HDL-C: High-density lipoprotein (“good” cholesterol)
- TG: Triglycerides (a type of blood fat)
- Total-C: Total cholesterol

Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.
Atorvastatin helps lower LDL cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') and triglyceride levels, and increases HDL cholesterol ('good cholesterol') levels, to improve your overall lipid profile.
Atorvastatin calcium belongs to a class of medications called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly referred to as statins.
Atrovastatin tablets are taken once daily with or without food.

candidate_edges.subject: Atorvastatin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to prevent or lower the risk of the medical event or condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
When cholesterol and fats build up along your artery walls, in a process called atherosclerosis, they narrow the blood vessels and reduce blood and oxygen flow to your heart, brain, and other parts of your body. By slowing cholesterol production, atorvastatin helps prevent this buildup to keep blood flowing more freely to vital organs.
Lowering your blood level of cholesterol and fats with atorvastatin may help prevent heart disease, angina (chest pain), strokes, and heart attacks.
Your healthcare provider will check your blood lipid levels regularly to assess how well your treatment is working. These measurements include:
- LDL-C: Low-density lipoprotein (“bad” cholesterol)
- HDL-C: High-density lipoprotein (“good” cholesterol)
- TG: Triglycerides (a type of blood fat)
- Total-C: Total cholesterol

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Atorvastatin FDA-approved uses:
To reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in adults with:
- Multiple risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD), but without established CHD. Use: to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, revascularization procedures, and angina.
- Type 2 diabetes and multiple risk factors for CHD, without established CHD Use: to help reduce the risk of MI and stroke.
- Adults with clinically evident CHD: Use: To reduce the risk of non-fatal MI, fatal and non-fatal stroke, revascularization procedures, hospitalization for congestive heart failure, and angina.
As an adjunct to diet to lower LDL-C:
- Adults with primary hyperlipidemia.
- Adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH).
As an adjunct to other LDL-lowering therapies:
- For adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
As an adjunct to diet for additional lipid disorders in adults:
- Primary dysbetalipoproteinemia.
- Hypertriglyceridemia.

graph_edge.subject: Atorvastatin
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug decreases the level of the substance or biomarker specified by the object entity in the body.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Atorvastatin works by selectively blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the key enzyme the liver uses to produce cholesterol. By slowing this process, it reduces cholesterol production in the liver and increases the number of LDL receptors on liver cells, which helps remove more LDL (“bad”) cholesterol from the bloodstream.
As a result, it lowers overall LDL levels, decreases the number of LDL particles, and improves the body’s ability to clear cholesterol.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take atorvastatin if you have liver disease or cirrhosis.
Atorvastatin can cause the breakdown of muscle tissue, which can lead to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, or dark urine.
Serious drug interactions can occur when certain medicines are used together with atorvastatin. Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you use now, and any medicine you start or stop using.
Avoid eating foods that are high in fat or cholesterol. Atorvastatin will not be as effective in lowering your cholesterol if you do not follow a cholesterol-lowering diet plan.
Atorvastatin is only part of a complete program of treatment that also includes diet, exercise, and weight control. Follow your diet, medication, and exercise routines very closely.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take atorvastatin tablet once daily with or without food. Many people ask when to take atorvastatin morning or night? It can be taken any time of the day, but try and take it at the same time each day.
Take the liquid medicine on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before a meal or 2 hours after a meal. Shake the oral suspension (liquid). Measure a dose with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Take atorvastatin exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Do not change your dose or stop taking any of your medications without your doctor's advice.
It may take up to 2 weeks before your cholesterol levels improve, and you may need frequent blood tests. Even if you have no symptoms, tests can help your doctor determine if this medicine is effective.
Your treatment may also include diet, exercise, weight control, and blood tests.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Throw away in the trash any unused liquid 60 days after opening the bottle.

By slowing this process, it reduces cholesterol production in the liver and increases the number of LDL receptors on liver cells, which helps remove more LDL (“bad”) cholesterol from the bloodstream.
As a result, it lowers overall LDL levels, decreases the number of LDL particles, and improves the body’s ability to clear cholesterol.

Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.
Atorvastatin helps lower LDL cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') and triglyceride levels, and increases HDL cholesterol ('good cholesterol') levels, to improve your overall lipid profile.
Atorvastatin calcium belongs to a class of medications called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly referred to as statins.
Atrovastatin tablets are taken once daily with or without food.

Lowering your blood level of cholesterol and fats with atorvastatin may help prevent heart disease, angina (chest pain), strokes, and heart attacks.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
You should not take atorvastatin if you have liver disease or cirrhosis.
Atorvastatin can cause the breakdown of muscle tissue, which can lead to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, or dark urine.
Serious drug interactions can occur when certain medicines are used together with atorvastatin. Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you use now, and any medicine you start or stop using.
Avoid eating foods that are high in fat or cholesterol. Atorvastatin will not be as effective in lowering your cholesterol if you do not follow a cholesterol-lowering diet plan.
Atorvastatin is only part of a complete program of treatment that also includes diet, exercise, and weight control. Follow your diet, medication, and exercise routines very closely.

candidate_edges.object: taken once daily with or without food
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.
Atorvastatin helps lower LDL cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') and triglyceride levels, and increases HDL cholesterol ('good cholesterol') levels, to improve your overall lipid profile.
Atorvastatin calcium belongs to a class of medications called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly referred to as statins.
Atrovastatin tablets are taken once daily with or without food.

candidate_edges.subject: Atorvastatin liquid
candidate_edges.object: take at least 2 hours after a meal
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take atorvastatin tablet once daily with or without food. Many people ask when to take atorvastatin morning or night? It can be taken any time of the day, but try and take it at the same time each day.
Take the liquid medicine on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before a meal or 2 hours after a meal. Shake the oral suspension (liquid). Measure a dose with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Take atorvastatin exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Do not change your dose or stop taking any of your medications without your doctor's advice.
It may take up to 2 weeks before your cholesterol levels improve, and you may need frequent blood tests. Even if you have no symptoms, tests can help your doctor determine if this medicine is effective.
Your treatment may also include diet, exercise, weight control, and blood tests.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Throw away in the trash any unused liquid 60 days after opening the bottle.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is typically prescribed at the dose or dosing regimen specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Recommended Dosage in Adult Patients The recommended starting dosage of Lipitor is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily. The dosage range is 10 mg to 80 mg once daily. Patients who require a reduction in LDL-C greater than 45% may be started at 40 mg once daily.
Recommended Dosage in Pediatric Patients 10 Years of Age and Older with HeFH The recommended starting dosage of Lipitor is 10 mg once daily. The dosage range is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily.
Recommended Dosage in Pediatric Patients 10 Years of Age and Older with HoFH The recommended starting dosage of Lipitor is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily. The dosage range is 10 mg to 80 mg once daily.
Comments: Assess LDL-C when clinically appropriate, as early as 4 weeks after initiating Lipitor, and adjust the dosage if necessary.
This medicine is available as: atorvastatin 10 mg tablets, atorvastatin 20 mg tablets, atorvastatin 40 mg tablet, 80 mg tablets.
The original brand name of atorvastatin was Lipitor, and now it is also available as a generic. Atorvastatin calcium oral suspension is also available as the brand Aorvaliq 20mg/5ml.

You should not take atorvastatin if you have liver disease or cirrhosis.

candidate_edges.subject: Levothyroxine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is sold under or known by the generic (non-proprietary) name specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.

candidate_edges.subject: Levothyroxine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is not indicated or used to treat the condition or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine. Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis.
Older adults and people with heart disease are usually started on a lower dose, because too much thyroid hormone can cause an irregular heartbeat (most commonly atrial fibrillation), angina, or other heart problems. Tell your doctor if you develop chest pain, breathlessness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures. This is more likely after menopause. Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels.
Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma. Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.

Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small. Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development. You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions. Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack.

graph_edge.subject: Levothyroxine
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is not indicated or used to treat the condition or situation specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.

candidate_edges.subject: Levothyroxine injection
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.

Levothyroxine should not be used to treat obesity or weight problems. Dangerous side effects or death can occur from the misuse of this medicine, especially if you are taking any other weight-loss medications or appetite suppressants.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small. Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development. Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust it gradually based on blood tests.
You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions. Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Having hypothyroidism during pregnancy may increase the risk of miscarriage, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, or premature birth, and untreated hypothyroidism can affect the baby's brain development. The benefit of treating hypothyroidism outweighs these risks, and levothyroxine should not be stopped during pregnancy.
Your dose needs are often higher during pregnancy. Your doctor will check your thyroid blood tests as soon as your pregnancy is confirmed and at least once in each trimester, and will usually put you back on your pre-pregnancy dose straight after you give birth, with another blood test 4 to 8 weeks later.
Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Levothyroxine passes into breast milk, but no harmful effects on breastfed babies have been reported. Treating hypothyroidism properly may also help milk supply if it is low. Your dose needs may be different while you are nursing.

Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Does metformin work for weight loss?:
Yes. Metformin can lead to a modest weight loss, though results vary, and it's generally smaller amount of weight loss than what's seen with medications specifically approved for weight loss.
In the landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomized controlled trial in people at high risk for diabetes, participants taking metformin lost more weight than those on placebo. Metformin patients lost 2.7% of body weight after one year, compared to 0.43% for placebo, and 2.1% after two years compared to essentially no change (0.02%) for placebo. Looking at it another way, 29% of people on metformin lost at least 5% of their starting body weight after one year, versus just 13% on placebo, a gap that held up at the two-year mark (26% vs. 14%).
Metformin is not FDA-approved for weight loss.

Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.
Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides.
Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity. Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug carries an official boxed (black box) safety warning about the risk specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea

If you need to have surgery or any type of x-ray or CT scan using a dye that is injected into your veins, you may need to temporarily stop taking metformin. Be sure your caregivers know ahead of time that you are using this medication.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- kidney disease (your kidney function may need to be checked before you take this medicine);
- high ketone levels in your blood or urine;
- heart disease, congestive heart failure;
- liver disease or liver impairment
- if you also use insulin, or other oral diabetes medications.
You may develop lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood. This may be more likely if you have other medical conditions, a severe infection, chronic alcoholism, or if you are 65 or older. Ask your doctor about your risk.
Metformin immediate release tablets should not be given to a child younger than 10 years old.
This medicine should not be used for type 1 diabetes.

Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) by itself. However, hypoglycemia can happen if you do not eat enough, if you drink alcohol, or if you take other medicines to lower blood sugar.
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metformin: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
This medicine can rarely cause patients to develop lactic acidosis, which can be fatal. See the “Warnings - Boxed Warning” for more details.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of liver problems, such as upper stomach pain, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools, or yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice).

candidate_edges.subject: metformin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug produces its therapeutic effect through the biological mechanism specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text: Metformin is prescribed to manage polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) because it improves how the body responds to insulin. PCOS affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age and is often marked by insulin resistance, in which the body doesn't respond well to insulin, prompting the pancreas to produce more. This excess insulin drives up androgen (male hormone) production, worsening symptoms like irregular periods, infertility, acne, and excess hair growth. Metformin helps by lowering insulin levels, decreasing the liver's glucose production, improving glucose uptake by muscles, and reducing circulating androgen levels as well, which can support more regular ovulation and menstrual cycles.

candidate_edges.subject: metformin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used together with the other treatment or lifestyle measure specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.
Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides.
Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity. Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Your doctor may prescribe a glucagon injection kit in case you have severe hypoglycemia. Be sure your family or close friends know how to give you this injection in an emergency.

Metformin is only part of a complete treatment program that may also include diet, exercise, weight control, regular blood sugar testing, and special medical care. Follow your doctor's instructions very closely.

graph_edge.subject: metformin hydrochloride tablets
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the adverse effect or symptom specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Common side effects:
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.
Less common side effects were abnormal stools, hypoglycemia, myalgia, lightheadedness, dyspnea, nail disorder, rash, increased sweating, taste disorder, chest discomfort, chills, flu syndrome, flushing, and palpitation, which occurred between 1% and less than 5% of patients.
Taking your medicine with meals can help reduce these side effects, and you may find the slow-release tablets reduce gastric side effects. Tell your doctor if the side effects bother you a lot, last for more than a few weeks, come back after they've gone away, or start later in therapy. You may need a lower dose or need to stop taking the medicine for a short period or for good.

candidate_edges.subject: lactic acidosis
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The medical condition specified by the subject entity is characterized by the symptom or sign described by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
If you need to have surgery or any type of x-ray or CT scan using a dye that is injected into your veins, you may need to temporarily stop taking metformin. Be sure your caregivers know ahead of time that you are using this medication.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- kidney disease (your kidney function may need to be checked before you take this medicine);
- high ketone levels in your blood or urine;
- heart disease, congestive heart failure;
- liver disease or liver impairment
- if you also use insulin, or other oral diabetes medications.
You may develop lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood. This may be more likely if you have other medical conditions, a severe infection, chronic alcoholism, or if you are 65 or older. Ask your doctor about your risk.
Metformin immediate release tablets should not be given to a child younger than 10 years old.
This medicine should not be used for type 1 diabetes.

- Before starting treatment, assess renal function with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
- Do not use this medicine in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/minute/1.73 m 2
- It is not recommended to start metformin tablets in patients with eGFR between 30 to 45 mL/minute/1.73 m 2
- While taking this medicine, assess the risk/benefit of continuing if eGFR falls below 45 mL/minute/1.73 m 2
- If eGFR falls below 30 mL/minute/1.73 m 2 discontinue this medication
Metformin immediate release tablets are available as 500 mg, 850 mg, and 1,000 mg tablets.
Hepatic Impairment:
Avoid use in patients with hepatic impairment.

Initial dose: 500 to 1000 mg orally once a day Dose titration: Increase in 500 mg increments weekly as tolerated Maximum dose: 2000 mg/day

Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea

Controlling diabetes is very important during pregnancy, and having high blood sugar may cause complications in both the mother and the baby. Tell your doctor if you become pregnant while taking metformin.
Metformin may stimulate ovulation in some women and may increase the risk of unintended pregnancy. Talk to your doctor about your risk.
Breastfeeding:
Talk to your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. Metformin can pass into your breast milk. Your healthcare provider will be able to advise you about the best way to feed your baby while you take this medicine.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common side effects:
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.
Less common side effects were abnormal stools, hypoglycemia, myalgia, lightheadedness, dyspnea, nail disorder, rash, increased sweating, taste disorder, chest discomfort, chills, flu syndrome, flushing, and palpitation, which occurred between 1% and less than 5% of patients.
Taking your medicine with meals can help reduce these side effects, and you may find the slow-release tablets reduce gastric side effects. Tell your doctor if the side effects bother you a lot, last for more than a few weeks, come back after they've gone away, or start later in therapy. You may need a lower dose or need to stop taking the medicine for a short period or for good.

candidate_edges.subject: metformin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
If you need to have surgery or any type of x-ray or CT scan using a dye that is injected into your veins, you may need to temporarily stop taking metformin. Be sure your caregivers know ahead of time that you are using this medication.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- kidney disease (your kidney function may need to be checked before you take this medicine);
- high ketone levels in your blood or urine;
- heart disease, congestive heart failure;
- liver disease or liver impairment
- if you also use insulin, or other oral diabetes medications.

Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea

Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common side effects:
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.
Less common side effects were abnormal stools, hypoglycemia, myalgia, lightheadedness, dyspnea, nail disorder, rash, increased sweating, taste disorder, chest discomfort, chills, flu syndrome, flushing, and palpitation, which occurred between 1% and less than 5% of patients.
Taking your medicine with meals can help reduce these side effects, and you may find the slow-release tablets reduce gastric side effects. Tell your doctor if the side effects bother you a lot, last for more than a few weeks, come back after they've gone away, or start later in therapy. You may need a lower dose or need to stop taking the medicine for a short period or for good.

Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).

- very weak and tired

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.
Amlodipine besylate is available as:
- Amlodipine 5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 10 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 2.5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL solution (Norliqva)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL oral suspension (Katerzia)
- Amlodipine single-dose powder for oral solution (Sdamlo).

Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.
Amlodipine besylate is available as:
- Amlodipine 5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 10 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 2.5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL solution (Norliqva)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL oral suspension (Katerzia)
- Amlodipine single-dose powder for oral solution (Sdamlo).

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take amlodipine if you are allergic to it.
To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- severe narrowing of a certain valve in your heart (aortic stenosis), or other heart problems;
- coronary artery disease (clogged arteries); or
- liver disease.
It is not known if amlodipine will harm an unborn baby. However, having high blood pressure during pregnancy may cause complications or medical problems in both mother and baby. The benefit of treating hypertension may outweigh any risks to the baby.
Do not breastfeed while taking amlodipine. You can stop breastfeeding or take a different medicine.

Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.
Amlodipine besylate is available as:
- Amlodipine 5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 10 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 2.5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL solution (Norliqva)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL oral suspension (Katerzia)
- Amlodipine single-dose powder for oral solution (Sdamlo).

Usual Pediatric Dose for Hypertension:

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.
Amlodipine besylate is available as:
- Amlodipine 5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 10 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 2.5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL solution (Norliqva)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL oral suspension (Katerzia)
- Amlodipine single-dose powder for oral solution (Sdamlo).

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems. In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure. These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems. In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure. These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.

You may take lisinopril with or without food.
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often and you may need frequent blood tests.
Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery.

If you have high blood pressure, keep using lisinopril even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
Store tightly closed at room temperature, away from moisture and heat. Do not freeze.

Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems. In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure. These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.

graph_edge.subject: Losartan
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Losartan is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children at least 6 years old.
Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).
Losartan may not decrease the risk of stroke in African Americans who have these conditions.
Losartan is also used to treat kidney disease in people who have type 2 diabetes (condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood) and high blood pressure.
Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin II receptor antagonists. It works by blocking the action of certain natural substances that tighten the blood vessels, allowing the blood to flow more smoothly and the heart to pump more efficiently.

Do not use losartan if you are pregnant, and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. It can cause injury or death to the unborn baby.
If you have diabetes, do not use losartan together with any medication that contains aliskiren (a blood pressure medicine).
You may also need to avoid taking losartan with aliskiren if you have kidney disease.
In rare cases, this medicine can cause a condition that results in the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue, leading to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, and dark colored urine.

Losartan is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children at least 6 years old.
Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).
Losartan may not decrease the risk of stroke in African Americans who have these conditions.
Losartan is also used to treat kidney disease in people who have type 2 diabetes (condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood) and high blood pressure.
Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin II receptor antagonists. It works by blocking the action of certain natural substances that tighten the blood vessels, allowing the blood to flow more smoothly and the heart to pump more efficiently.

- liver disease; or

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug enhances or potentiates the effect of the substance or condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
The interactions that matter most are medicines that also slow the heart and medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which raises metoprolol levels in your blood.
- Digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, and verapamil. These all slow the heart's electrical signal and heart rate. Taking them with metoprolol raises the risk of a very slow heartbeat.
- Clonidine, when stopping either medicine. If you take both, the metoprolol is stopped several days before clonidine is slowly withdrawn, because beta blockers can worsen the blood pressure rebound that follows clonidine withdrawal.
- Quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and propafenone. These strong CYP2D6 blockers double the amount of metoprolol in your blood. Quinidine tripled levels of one form of metoprolol and doubled how long it lasted. Weaker CYP2D6 blockers are likely to raise levels too.
- Reserpine and MAO inhibitors. These deplete adrenaline-type chemicals and can add to metoprolol's effect, causing low blood pressure or a marked slowing of the heart.

The interactions that matter most are medicines that also slow the heart and medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which raises metoprolol levels in your blood.
- Digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, and verapamil. These all slow the heart's electrical signal and heart rate. Taking them with metoprolol raises the risk of a very slow heartbeat.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack. If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond. This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.
Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you.
- Asthma or other breathing problems. Beta blockers can tighten the airways. Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand.
- Heart failure. Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased. Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness.
- A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart. This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Your heart rate should be monitored.

- Wheezing or trouble breathing

- Cold, pale, or blue fingers and toes, or pain in your legs when you walk
- Confusion, hallucinations, or memory problems
- Yellowing of your skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver inflammation
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Extended-release metoprolol is the only form approved for children, and only for high blood pressure in children aged 6 years and older. The starting dose is 1 mg for each kilogram of body weight once a day, up to a maximum first dose of 50 mg. Doses above 2 mg/kg, or above 200 mg a day, have not been studied. Extended-release metoprolol has not been studied in children under 6 years.
Dose adjustments:
- Liver problems. Start at a lower dose than usual and increase slowly.
- Kidney problems. No dose reduction is needed.
- Older adults. A low starting dose is generally used, because liver, kidney, and heart function are more often reduced and other medicines are more often involved.
- Switching between forms. When changing from immediate-release to extended-release metoprolol, the same total daily dose is used.

candidate_edges.subject: Metoprolol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

candidate_edges.subject: Metoprolol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack. If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond. This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.
Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you.
- Asthma or other breathing problems. Beta blockers can tighten the airways. Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand.
- Heart failure. Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased. Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness.
- A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart. This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Your heart rate should be monitored.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Extended-release metoprolol is the only form approved for children, and only for high blood pressure in children aged 6 years and older. The starting dose is 1 mg for each kilogram of body weight once a day, up to a maximum first dose of 50 mg. Doses above 2 mg/kg, or above 200 mg a day, have not been studied. Extended-release metoprolol has not been studied in children under 6 years.
Dose adjustments:
- Liver problems. Start at a lower dose than usual and increase slowly.
- Kidney problems. No dose reduction is needed.
- Older adults. A low starting dose is generally used, because liver, kidney, and heart function are more often reduced and other medicines are more often involved.
- Switching between forms. When changing from immediate-release to extended-release metoprolol, the same total daily dose is used.

The interactions that matter most are medicines that also slow the heart and medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which raises metoprolol levels in your blood.
- Digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, and verapamil. These all slow the heart's electrical signal and heart rate. Taking them with metoprolol raises the risk of a very slow heartbeat.
- Clonidine, when stopping either medicine. If you take both, the metoprolol is stopped several days before clonidine is slowly withdrawn, because beta blockers can worsen the blood pressure rebound that follows clonidine withdrawal.
- Quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and propafenone. These strong CYP2D6 blockers double the amount of metoprolol in your blood. Quinidine tripled levels of one form of metoprolol and doubled how long it lasted. Weaker CYP2D6 blockers are likely to raise levels too.
- Reserpine and MAO inhibitors. These deplete adrenaline-type chemicals and can add to metoprolol's effect, causing low blood pressure or a marked slowing of the heart.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Metoprolol crosses the placenta and passes into breast milk in small amounts. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding.
Studies published to date have not shown a link between metoprolol taken in pregnancy and major birth defects or miscarriage. Reports on growth restriction, early birth, and death around the time of birth have been inconsistent, and those studies have limitations that make them hard to interpret. Untreated high blood pressure and untreated heart failure in pregnancy carry their own serious risks for both mother and baby.
Babies born to mothers taking metoprolol may have low blood pressure, low blood sugar, a slow heartbeat, or slow breathing, so they are watched after birth.
The amount of metoprolol a breastfed baby receives is estimated at 0.05 mg to under 1 mg a day, which is about 0.5% to 2% of the mother's weight-adjusted dose. No side effects in breastfed babies have been identified. Babies are still monitored for a slow heartbeat and for signs such as unusual sleepiness.

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. graph_edge.subject: Rosuvastatin
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

- to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as death from cardiovascular disease, heart attack, stroke, or the need for procedures to improve blood flow to the heart called arterial revascularization, in adults at increased risk for these events.

- along with diet for the treatment of adults with: primary dysbetalipoproteinemia (an inherited condition that causes high levels of cholesterol and fat). hypertriglyceridemia.

candidate_edges.subject: Rosuvastatin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Common side effects:
The most common side effects may include headache, nausea, muscle aches and pains, weakness, and constipation.
Serious side effects:
Rosuvastatin may cause serious side effects, including:
- Muscle pain, tenderness and weakness (myopathy). Muscle problems, including muscle breakdown, can be serious in some people and rarely cause kidney damage that can lead to death. Tell your doctor right away if: you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you have a fever or feel more tired than usual, while you take this medicine. you have muscle problems that do not go away even after your doctor has told you to stop taking this medicine. Your doctor may do further tests to diagnose the cause of your muscle problems. Your chances of getting muscle problems are higher if you: are taking certain other medicines while you take rosuvastatin are 65 years of age or older are of Asian descent have thyroid problems (hypothyroidism) that are not controlled have kidney problems are taking higher doses of this medicine

- Liver problems. Your doctor may do blood tests to check your liver before you start taking this medicine and if you have symptoms of liver problems while you are taking it. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following symptoms of liver problems: feel unusually tired or weak loss of appetite upper belly pain dark urine yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes
