candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common insulin glargine side effects may include low blood sugar, swelling, weight gain, allergic reaction, itching, rash, or thickening or hollowing of the skin where you injected the medicine (lipodystrophy).
Serious insulin glargine side effects
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of insulin allergy: redness or swelling where an injection was given, itchy skin rash over the entire body, trouble breathing, fast heartbeats, feeling like you might pass out, or swelling in your tongue or throat.
Insulin glargine may cause other serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- rapid weight gain, swelling in your feet or ankles;
- shortness of breath; or
- low blood potassium--leg cramps, constipation, irregular heartbeats, fluttering in your chest, increased thirst or urination, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness or limp feeling.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

graph_edge.subject: Insulin glargine
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug should be stored according to the instruction specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Storing unopened (not in use) insulin glargine:
- Refrigerate at 36°F–46°F (2°C–8°C)
- Do NOT use after the expiration date.
Storing opened (in use) insulin glargine:
- Storage once in use varies for different brands of insulin glargine. For storage information for the different brands of insulin glargine while in use, check the prescribing information.
General storage information
- Keep this medicine in its original container protected from heat and light.
- Do not store an injection pen with the needle attached. Do not reuse a needle or syringe. Place them in a puncture-proof "sharps" container and dispose of it following state or local laws. Keep out of the reach of children and pets.

Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Take empagliflozin once a day in the morning, with or without food.
Your blood sugar will need to be checked often, and you may also need to test the level of ketones in your urine. Empagliflozin can cause life-threatening ketoacidosis (too much acid in the blood). Even if your blood sugar is normal, contact your doctor if a urine test shows that you have high ketones in the urine.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injection in case of severe hypoglycemia.
You may get dehydrated during prolonged illness. Call your doctor if you are sick with vomiting or diarrhea.

Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Take empagliflozin once a day in the morning, with or without food.
Your blood sugar will need to be checked often, and you may also need to test the level of ketones in your urine. Empagliflozin can cause life-threatening ketoacidosis (too much acid in the blood). Even if your blood sugar is normal, contact your doctor if a urine test shows that you have high ketones in the urine.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injection in case of severe hypoglycemia.
You may get dehydrated during prolonged illness. Call your doctor if you are sick with vomiting or diarrhea.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Take empagliflozin once a day in the morning, with or without food.
Your blood sugar will need to be checked often, and you may also need to test the level of ketones in your urine. Empagliflozin can cause life-threatening ketoacidosis (too much acid in the blood). Even if your blood sugar is normal, contact your doctor if a urine test shows that you have high ketones in the urine.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injection in case of severe hypoglycemia.
You may get dehydrated during prolonged illness. Call your doctor if you are sick with vomiting or diarrhea.

Call your doctor at once if you have signs of a serious side effect, such as stomach pain, vomiting, tiredness, or trouble breathing.
Tell your doctor if you are sick with vomiting or diarrhea, or if you eat or drink less than usual.
Empagliflozin can cause serious infections around the penis or vagina. Get medical help right away if you have burning, itching, odor, discharge, pain, tenderness, redness or swelling of the genital or rectal area, fever, or if you don't feel well.

candidate_edges.subject: Furosemide
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is a member of the pharmacological or therapeutic drug class specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Furosemide is a loop diuretic used to treat fluid retention (edema) in people with congestive heart failure, liver disease, or a chronic kidney disorder such as nephrotic syndrome. Furosemide is also used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).
Furosemide works by increasing the amount of urine the body makes, which helps reduce swelling and symptoms of fluid retention and helps lower high blood pressure. Furosemide tablets are sometimes called water pills as they increase how much you urinate.
Furosemide is also known as frusemide in some countries. It has been available in the United States since the 1960s and comes as tablets (Lasix), an oral liquid, an intravenous solution, and subcutaneous injections and infusions that can be given at home (Furoscix, Lasix ONYU).

candidate_edges.subject: Furosemide
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug produces its therapeutic effect through the biological mechanism specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use furosemide if you are unable to urinate.
Using more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective. High doses of this medicine may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Before using this medicine, tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, enlarged prostate, urination problems, cirrhosis or other liver disease, an electrolyte imbalance, high cholesterol, gout, lupus, diabetes, or an allergy to sulfa drugs.
Tell your doctor if you have recently had an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) or any type of scan using a radioactive dye that is injected into your veins. Do not take more of this medication than is recommended.
If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep using this medicine even if you feel fine. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
Furosemide is a potent diuretic which, if given in excessive amounts, can lead to a profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion. Careful medical supervision is required, and the dose schedule must be adjusted to the individual patient's needs.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines. Some drugs should not be used with furosemide.

Common side effects:
Common furosemide side effects may include:
- diarrhea, constipation, loss of appetite
- numbness or tingling
- headache, dizziness
- blurred vision
- redness, bruising, swelling, or pain where a subcutaneous dose is given.
Serious furosemide side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to furosemide (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Furosemide may cause other serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out
- ringing in your ears, hearing loss
- muscle spasms or contractions
- pale skin, easy bruising, unusual bleeding
- high blood sugar, with increased thirst, increased urination, dry mouth, or fruity breath odor
- kidney problems, with swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common side effects:
Common furosemide side effects may include:
- diarrhea, constipation, loss of appetite
- numbness or tingling
- headache, dizziness
- blurred vision
- redness, bruising, swelling, or pain where a subcutaneous dose is given.
Serious furosemide side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to furosemide (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Furosemide may cause other serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out
- ringing in your ears, hearing loss
- muscle spasms or contractions
- pale skin, easy bruising, unusual bleeding
- high blood sugar, with increased thirst, increased urination, dry mouth, or fruity breath odor
- kidney problems, with swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath

candidate_edges.object: reduces swelling and symptoms of fluid retention
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Furosemide is a loop diuretic used to treat fluid retention (edema) in people with congestive heart failure, liver disease, or a chronic kidney disorder such as nephrotic syndrome. Furosemide is also used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).
Furosemide works by increasing the amount of urine the body makes, which helps reduce swelling and symptoms of fluid retention and helps lower high blood pressure. Furosemide tablets are sometimes called water pills as they increase how much you urinate.
Furosemide is also known as frusemide in some countries. It has been available in the United States since the 1960s and comes as tablets (Lasix), an oral liquid, an intravenous solution, and subcutaneous injections and infusions that can be given at home (Furoscix, Lasix ONYU).

- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.

Common furosemide side effects may include:

Furosemide is a loop diuretic used to treat fluid retention (edema) in people with congestive heart failure, liver disease, or a chronic kidney disorder such as nephrotic syndrome. Furosemide is also used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use furosemide if you are unable to urinate.
Using more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective. High doses of this medicine may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Before using this medicine, tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, enlarged prostate, urination problems, cirrhosis or other liver disease, an electrolyte imbalance, high cholesterol, gout, lupus, diabetes, or an allergy to sulfa drugs.
Tell your doctor if you have recently had an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) or any type of scan using a radioactive dye that is injected into your veins. Do not take more of this medication than is recommended.
If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep using this medicine even if you feel fine. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
Furosemide is a potent diuretic which, if given in excessive amounts, can lead to a profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion. Careful medical supervision is required, and the dose schedule must be adjusted to the individual patient's needs.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines. Some drugs should not be used with furosemide.

Meloxicam is used to relieve pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness caused by osteoarthritis (arthritis caused by a breakdown of the lining of the joints) and rheumatoid arthritis (arthritis caused by swelling of the lining of the joints).
Meloxicam is also used to relieve the pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness caused by juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (a type of arthritis that affects children) in children 2 years of age and older.
IV meloxicam (brands Anjeso [discontinued], Qamzova, Xifyrm) is used for moderate to severe pain in adults, alone or in combination with non-NSAID analgesics.
Vivlodex capsules [discontinued] are only for use in adults. Qmiiz ODT (orally disintegrating tablet) [discontinued] is for adults and children weighing at least 132 pounds (60 kilograms).
Generic meloxicam is available.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke, especially if you use it long term or take high doses, or if you have heart disease. Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking meloxicam after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to. You may have an increased risk of another heart attack if you take this medicine after a recent heart attack.
Get emergency medical help if you have chest pain, weakness, shortness of breath, slurred speech, or problems with vision or balance.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal. These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Call your doctor at once if you have symptoms of stomach bleeding, such as black, bloody, or tarry stools, or coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Avoid smoking and drinking alcohol, as they also increase your risk of stomach bleeding.

If you need to take this medicine for more than 2 days when you are between 20 and 30 weeks of pregnancy, your doctor may need to monitor the amount of fluid around your baby. You should not take meloxicam after about 30 weeks of pregnancy.
Planning a pregnancy:
Meloxicam may cause a delay in ovulation (the release of an egg from an ovary). You should not take this medicine if you are undergoing fertility treatment or are otherwise trying to get pregnant.
Breastfeeding:
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the serious or potentially dangerous adverse effect specified by the object entity that requires medical attention.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke, especially if you use it long term or take high doses, or if you have heart disease. Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking meloxicam after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to. You may have an increased risk of another heart attack if you take this medicine after a recent heart attack.
Get emergency medical help if you have chest pain, weakness, shortness of breath, slurred speech, or problems with vision or balance.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal. These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Call your doctor at once if you have symptoms of stomach bleeding, such as black, bloody, or tarry stools, or coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Avoid smoking and drinking alcohol, as they also increase your risk of stomach bleeding.

Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a strong prescription combination pain medicine containing an opioid, hydrocodone, in addition to acetaminophen, which is used to manage moderate to moderately severe pain, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
An opioid pain medicine that can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a Schedule II controlled substance.
All branded hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, Hycet, Lorcet, Verdrocet, Xodol, Zamicet) have been discontinued, but generic hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets and oral solution is still available.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen first gained FDA approval on May 3, 1982.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should not exceed the maximum dose specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Adult Dose of Hydrocodone And Acetaminophen for Moderate to Severe Pain:
Hydrocodone 2.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet, Hydrocodone 5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 to 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 8 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg, Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 6 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 15 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours
Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 300 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 11.25 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 67.5 mL/24 hours
Comments:
- Doses should be individually titrated to provide adequate analgesia while minimizing adverse reactions.
- Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse, the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with individual patient treatment goals should be used.
- Monitor patients closely for respiratory depression within the first 24 to 72 hours of initiating therapy and following any increase in dose.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common Side Effects:
The possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen are constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and abdominal pain. Call your healthcare provider if you have any of these symptoms and they are severe.
Get emergency medical help if you have:
- Trouble breathing
- Shortness of breath
- Fast heartbeat
- Chest pain
- Swelling of your face, tongue, or throat
- Extreme drowsiness
- Light-headedness when changing positions
- Feeling faint
- Agitation
- High body temperature
- Trouble walking
- Stiff muscles
- Mental changes such as confusion.
These are not all the possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
candidate_edges.object: call healthcare provider if dose does not control pain
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
When taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen:
- Do not change your dose. Take hydrocodone and acetaminophen exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
- Take your prescribed dose every four to six hours at the same time every day. Do not take more than your prescribed dose. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- If taking the oral solution, always use a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup to correctly measure your dose. Never use a household teaspoon or tablespoon to measure your medicine.
- Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain, if your pain gets worse, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain. Do not take more medicine without first talking to your healthcare provider.
If you have been taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen regularly, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider.
After you stop taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, flush any unused tablets or oral solution down the toilet.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
candidate_edges.relation_definition: An overdose of the subject drug may cause the symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.

When taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen:
- Do not change your dose. Take hydrocodone and acetaminophen exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
- Take your prescribed dose every four to six hours at the same time every day. Do not take more than your prescribed dose. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- If taking the oral solution, always use a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup to correctly measure your dose. Never use a household teaspoon or tablespoon to measure your medicine.
- Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain, if your pain gets worse, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain. Do not take more medicine without first talking to your healthcare provider.
If you have been taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen regularly, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider.
After you stop taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, flush any unused tablets or oral solution down the toilet.

Adult Dose of Hydrocodone And Acetaminophen for Moderate to Severe Pain:
Hydrocodone 2.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet, Hydrocodone 5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 to 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 8 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg, Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 6 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 15 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours
Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 300 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 11.25 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 67.5 mL/24 hours
Comments:
- Doses should be individually titrated to provide adequate analgesia while minimizing adverse reactions.
- Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse, the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with individual patient treatment goals should be used.
- Monitor patients closely for respiratory depression within the first 24 to 72 hours of initiating therapy and following any increase in dose.

- Do not change your dose. Take hydrocodone and acetaminophen exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
- Take your prescribed dose every four to six hours at the same time every day. Do not take more than your prescribed dose. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- If taking the oral solution, always use a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup to correctly measure your dose. Never use a household teaspoon or tablespoon to measure your medicine.
- Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain, if your pain gets worse, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain. Do not take more medicine without first talking to your healthcare provider.

After you stop taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, flush any unused tablets or oral solution down the toilet.

Common Side Effects:
The possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen are constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and abdominal pain. Call your healthcare provider if you have any of these symptoms and they are severe.
Get emergency medical help if you have:
- Trouble breathing
- Shortness of breath
- Fast heartbeat
- Chest pain
- Swelling of your face, tongue, or throat
- Extreme drowsiness
- Light-headedness when changing positions
- Feeling faint
- Agitation
- High body temperature
- Trouble walking
- Stiff muscles
- Mental changes such as confusion.
These are not all the possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take hydrocodone and acetaminophen if you have:
- Severe asthma, trouble breathing, or other lung problems
- A bowel blockage or a narrowing of the stomach or intestines
- Signs of an allergy, such as a rash
- Are allergic to any of its ingredients.
Before taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of:
- Head injury, seizures
- Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
- Problems urinating
- Pancreas or gallbladder problems
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
- Pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Prolonged use of hydrocodone and acetaminophen during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated
- Breastfeeding. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen pass into breast milk and may harm your baby. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

Common Side Effects:
The possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen are constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and abdominal pain. Call your healthcare provider if you have any of these symptoms and they are severe.
Get emergency medical help if you have:
- Trouble breathing
- Shortness of breath
- Fast heartbeat
- Chest pain
- Swelling of your face, tongue, or throat
- Extreme drowsiness
- Light-headedness when changing positions
- Feeling faint
- Agitation
- High body temperature
- Trouble walking
- Stiff muscles
- Mental changes such as confusion.
These are not all the possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
candidate_edges.object: sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma
candidate_edges.relation_definition: An overdose of the subject drug may cause the symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.

Do not take hydrocodone and acetaminophen if you have:
- Severe asthma, trouble breathing, or other lung problems
- A bowel blockage or a narrowing of the stomach or intestines
- Signs of an allergy, such as a rash
- Are allergic to any of its ingredients.
Before taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of:
- Head injury, seizures
- Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
- Problems urinating
- Pancreas or gallbladder problems
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
- Pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Prolonged use of hydrocodone and acetaminophen during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated
- Breastfeeding. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen pass into breast milk and may harm your baby. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

Before taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of:

- Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
- Problems urinating
- Pancreas or gallbladder problems
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
When taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen:
- Do not change your dose. Take hydrocodone and acetaminophen exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
- Take your prescribed dose every four to six hours at the same time every day. Do not take more than your prescribed dose. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- If taking the oral solution, always use a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup to correctly measure your dose. Never use a household teaspoon or tablespoon to measure your medicine.
- Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain, if your pain gets worse, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain. Do not take more medicine without first talking to your healthcare provider.
If you have been taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen regularly, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider.
After you stop taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, flush any unused tablets or oral solution down the toilet.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
candidate_edges.relation_definition: An overdose of the subject drug may cause the symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.

graph_edge.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
graph_edge.object: 1 to 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is typically prescribed at the dose or dosing regimen specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Adult Dose of Hydrocodone And Acetaminophen for Moderate to Severe Pain:
Hydrocodone 2.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet, Hydrocodone 5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 to 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 8 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg, Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 6 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 15 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours
Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 300 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 11.25 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 67.5 mL/24 hours
Comments:
- Doses should be individually titrated to provide adequate analgesia while minimizing adverse reactions.
- Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse, the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with individual patient treatment goals should be used.
- Monitor patients closely for respiratory depression within the first 24 to 72 hours of initiating therapy and following any increase in dose.

The possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen are constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and abdominal pain. Call your healthcare provider if you have any of these symptoms and they are severe.
Get emergency medical help if you have:
- Trouble breathing
- Shortness of breath
- Fast heartbeat
- Chest pain
- Swelling of your face, tongue, or throat
- Extreme drowsiness
- Light-headedness when changing positions
- Feeling faint
- Agitation
- High body temperature
- Trouble walking
- Stiff muscles
- Mental changes such as confusion.
These are not all the possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a strong prescription combination pain medicine containing an opioid, hydrocodone, in addition to acetaminophen, which is used to manage moderate to moderately severe pain, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
An opioid pain medicine that can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a Schedule II controlled substance.
All branded hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, Hycet, Lorcet, Verdrocet, Xodol, Zamicet) have been discontinued, but generic hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets and oral solution is still available.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen first gained FDA approval on May 3, 1982.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
candidate_edges.relation_definition: An overdose of the subject drug may cause the symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.

- Do not change your dose. Take hydrocodone and acetaminophen exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
- Take your prescribed dose every four to six hours at the same time every day. Do not take more than your prescribed dose. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- If taking the oral solution, always use a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup to correctly measure your dose. Never use a household teaspoon or tablespoon to measure your medicine.
- Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain, if your pain gets worse, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain. Do not take more medicine without first talking to your healthcare provider.
If you have been taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen regularly, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider.
After you stop taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, flush any unused tablets or oral solution down the toilet.

- Fast heartbeat

- Light-headedness when changing positions
- Feeling faint
- Agitation
- High body temperature
- Trouble walking
- Stiff muscles
- Mental changes such as confusion.

Tell your doctor and pharmacist what prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are planning to take or are taking. They may interact with tirzepatide, and your doctor may need to change the doses of your medications or monitor you carefully for side effects.
Birth control pills may not work as well while receiving this medicine. Your doctor may suggest you use another form of birth control for 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide and for 4 weeks after each dose change.
Taking tirzepatide with other medicines to treat diabetes, such as sulfonylureas or insulin, may increase your risk of hypoglycemia. Talk to your doctor and pharmacist about low blood sugar and how to manage it.
This medicine delays gastric emptying and may alter the absorption of other orally administered medicines.

candidate_edges.subject: Mounjaro
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is sold under or known by the generic (non-proprietary) name specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease to Mounjaro (tirzepatide, up to 15 mg once weekly) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly, a GLP-1 medicine already approved to reduce cardiovascular risk, with a median follow-up of about 4 years.
- Cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke occurred in 12.1% of those taking Mounjaro compared with 13.0% of those taking dulaglutide (HR 0.92, 95.3% CI 0.83–1.01), meeting the trial's goal of non-inferiority but not demonstrating superiority.
- Death from any cause occurred in 8.5% of the Mounjaro group versus 10.1% of the dulaglutide group (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75–0.94), though this was not a primary endpoint and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it should be read as exploratory.
Because the comparator was an active medicine rather than placebo, these results describe how Mounjaro performs against another GLP-1, not how much it lowers risk compared with no treatment.

Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition. Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise. It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.

candidate_edges.subject: Mounjaro
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject result or measurement had the specified relative risk compared to a comparator.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease to Mounjaro (tirzepatide, up to 15 mg once weekly) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly, a GLP-1 medicine already approved to reduce cardiovascular risk, with a median follow-up of about 4 years.
- Cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke occurred in 12.1% of those taking Mounjaro compared with 13.0% of those taking dulaglutide (HR 0.92, 95.3% CI 0.83–1.01), meeting the trial's goal of non-inferiority but not demonstrating superiority.
- Death from any cause occurred in 8.5% of the Mounjaro group versus 10.1% of the dulaglutide group (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75–0.94), though this was not a primary endpoint and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it should be read as exploratory.
Because the comparator was an active medicine rather than placebo, these results describe how Mounjaro performs against another GLP-1, not how much it lowers risk compared with no treatment.

graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is a member of the pharmacological or therapeutic drug class specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common Side Effects:
The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Constipation
- Nausea (mild to moderate)
- Decreased appetite
- Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
- Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
- Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems. Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
- Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.

- Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

candidate_edges.object: unknown if causes thyroid tumors in people
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tirzepatide carries a Boxed Warning for the risk of possible thyroid tumors.
Possible Thyroid Tumors (Including Cancer):
Tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath. These may be symptoms of thyroid cancer. In studies with rats, tirzepatide and medicines that work like tirzepatide have caused thyroid tumors, including thyroid cancer. It is not known if tirzepatide will cause thyroid tumors, or a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in people.
Do not use tirzepatide if you or any of your family have ever had a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or if you have an endocrine system condition called Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

- Do not mix insulin and tirzepatide together in the same injection. You may give an injection of tirzepatide and insulin in the same body area, but not right next to each other.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose, which may be gradually increased, but not more than once every 4 weeks.
You may change the day of the week you use tirzepatide as long as there are at least three days between doses.
Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor.
Tirzepatide KwikPen:
The KwikPen contains 4 fixed doses, and one dose is injected weekly (subcutaneously).
- For your weekly dose, you need to turn the dose knob all the way until it stops AND the 1 icon is in the dose window.
- After 4 doses, throw away (discard) the Pen, including the unused medicine. The Pen will prevent you from dialing a full dose after you have given yourself 4 weekly doses. Do not inject the leftover medicine. Do not transfer the leftover medicine from your Pen into a syringe.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
- Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
- Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
- Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
- Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
- Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation. Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Usual Zepbound Dose for Weight Loss and OSA (Adult):
- Initial dose: 2.5 mg under the skin (subcutaneously) once a week.
- After 4 weeks: The dosage should be increased to 5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- Further dose increases: After at least 4 weeks on the current dose, the dosage may be increased in 2.5 mg increments.
- Recommended maintenance dose for weight loss: 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
- Recommended maintenance dose for OSA: 10 mg or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
- Maximum dose: 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Dose of Mounjaro for Type 2 Diabetes (Adults and Children 10 Years and Older):
- Initial dose: 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- If additional glycemic control is needed: Increase the dose in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
- Maximum dose (adults): 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- Maximum dose (children 10 years and older): 10 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- Comments: The starting dose and escalation schedule are designed to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal side effects.

- The same dosing and escalation schedule applies.
- Start at 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week and increase in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose, up to a maximum of 15 mg once a week.

How to Use Mounjaro:
- Give once weekly at any time of day, with or without meals.
- Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen or thigh. Another person may inject into the back of the upper arm. Rotate injection sites with each dose.
- Missed dose: Give as soon as possible within 4 days (96 hours). If more than 4 days have passed, skip the missed dose and give the next dose on the regularly scheduled day.
- The day of weekly administration can be changed, if necessary, as long as the time between the 2 doses is at least 3 days (72 hours).

- Give once weekly at any time of day, with or without meals.

candidate_edges.subject: Mounjaro
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is available in the pharmaceutical dosage form specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease to Mounjaro (tirzepatide, up to 15 mg once weekly) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly, a GLP-1 medicine already approved to reduce cardiovascular risk, with a median follow-up of about 4 years.
- Cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke occurred in 12.1% of those taking Mounjaro compared with 13.0% of those taking dulaglutide (HR 0.92, 95.3% CI 0.83–1.01), meeting the trial's goal of non-inferiority but not demonstrating superiority.
- Death from any cause occurred in 8.5% of the Mounjaro group versus 10.1% of the dulaglutide group (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75–0.94), though this was not a primary endpoint and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it should be read as exploratory.
Because the comparator was an active medicine rather than placebo, these results describe how Mounjaro performs against another GLP-1, not how much it lowers risk compared with no treatment.

- Maximum dose (children 10 years and older): 10 mg subcutaneously once a week.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease to Mounjaro (tirzepatide, up to 15 mg once weekly) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly, a GLP-1 medicine already approved to reduce cardiovascular risk, with a median follow-up of about 4 years.
- Cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke occurred in 12.1% of those taking Mounjaro compared with 13.0% of those taking dulaglutide (HR 0.92, 95.3% CI 0.83–1.01), meeting the trial's goal of non-inferiority but not demonstrating superiority.
- Death from any cause occurred in 8.5% of the Mounjaro group versus 10.1% of the dulaglutide group (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75–0.94), though this was not a primary endpoint and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it should be read as exploratory.
Because the comparator was an active medicine rather than placebo, these results describe how Mounjaro performs against another GLP-1, not how much it lowers risk compared with no treatment.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common Side Effects:
The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Constipation
- Nausea (mild to moderate)
- Decreased appetite
- Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
- Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
- Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems. Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
- Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.

candidate_edges.subject: Tirzepatide
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the adverse effect or symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
- Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
- Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
- Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
- Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
- Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation. Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

graph_edge.subject: Methylphenidate
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Methylphenidate may be habit-forming. Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death. Tell your doctor if you have had problems with drug or alcohol abuse.
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Methylphenidate may cause new or worsening psychosis (unusual thoughts or behavior), especially if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of heart problems - chest pain, feeling light-headed or short of breath; signs of psychosis - paranoia, aggression, new behavior problems, seeing or hearing things that are not real; signs of circulation problems - unexplained wounds on your fingers or toes.
Tell your doctor if you have a history of drug or alcohol addiction. Keep the medication where others cannot get to it.

graph_edge.subject: Methylphenidate
graph_edge.object: misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Methylphenidate may be habit-forming. Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death. Tell your doctor if you have had problems with drug or alcohol abuse.
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Methylphenidate may cause new or worsening psychosis (unusual thoughts or behavior), especially if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of heart problems - chest pain, feeling light-headed or short of breath; signs of psychosis - paranoia, aggression, new behavior problems, seeing or hearing things that are not real; signs of circulation problems - unexplained wounds on your fingers or toes.
Tell your doctor if you have a history of drug or alcohol addiction. Keep the medication where others cannot get to it.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tell your doctor if you also use opioid medicine, herbal products, or medicine for depression, mental illness, Parkinson's disease, migraine headaches, serious infections, or prevention of nausea and vomiting. An interaction with methylphenidate could cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome.
Tell your doctor if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
- depression, mental illness, bipolar disorder, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts or actions;
- blood circulation problems in the hands or feet;
- alcoholism or drug addiction; or
- if you take Adhansia - an allergy to aspirin or yellow food dye.
- phenylketonuria (PKU), as some chewable tablets contain phenylalanine.
To make sure methylphenidate is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have::
- problems with the esophagus, stomach, or intestines; or
- seizures, epilepsy, or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG).

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tell your doctor if you also use opioid medicine, herbal products, or medicine for depression, mental illness, Parkinson's disease, migraine headaches, serious infections, or prevention of nausea and vomiting. An interaction with methylphenidate could cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome.
Tell your doctor if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
- depression, mental illness, bipolar disorder, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts or actions;
- blood circulation problems in the hands or feet;
- alcoholism or drug addiction; or
- if you take Adhansia - an allergy to aspirin or yellow food dye.

To make sure methylphenidate is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have::
- problems with the esophagus, stomach, or intestines; or
- seizures, epilepsy, or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG).

Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.

You may take methylphenidate with or without food, but take it the same way each time.
Swallow the extended-release capsule or tablet whole and do not crush, chew, or break it.
If you cannot swallow an extended-release CAPSULE whole, open it and mix the medicine with soft food such as applesauce, pudding or yogurt. Swallow the mixture right away WITHOUT CHEWING.

candidate_edges.subject: Methylphenidate
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Methylphenidate may be habit-forming. Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death. Tell your doctor if you have had problems with drug or alcohol abuse.
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Methylphenidate may cause new or worsening psychosis (unusual thoughts or behavior), especially if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of heart problems - chest pain, feeling light-headed or short of breath; signs of psychosis - paranoia, aggression, new behavior problems, seeing or hearing things that are not real; signs of circulation problems - unexplained wounds on your fingers or toes.
Tell your doctor if you have a history of drug or alcohol addiction. Keep the medication where others cannot get to it.

Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Methylphenidate may cause new or worsening psychosis (unusual thoughts or behavior), especially if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of heart problems - chest pain, feeling light-headed or short of breath; signs of psychosis - paranoia, aggression, new behavior problems, seeing or hearing things that are not real; signs of circulation problems - unexplained wounds on your fingers or toes.
Tell your doctor if you have a history of drug or alcohol addiction. Keep the medication where others cannot get to it.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Duloxetine is a selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressant (SSNRI). Duloxetine affects chemicals in the brain that may be unbalanced in people with depression.
Duloxetine is used to treat major depressive disorder in adults. It is also used to treat general anxiety disorder in adults and children who are at least 7 years old.
Duloxetine is also used in adults to treat nerve pain caused by diabetes (diabetic neuropathy), or chronic muscle or joint pain (such as low back pain and osteoarthritis pain).
Some brands of duloxetine are also used to treat fibromyalgia (a chronic pain disorder). Drizalma is for treating fibromyalgia only in adults. Cymbalta may be used to treat fibromyalgia in adults and children at least 13 years old.

People with depression or mental illness may have thoughts about suicide. Some young people may have increased suicidal thoughts when first starting a medicine to treat depression. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Your family or caregivers should also watch for sudden changes in your behavior.
Taking an SNRI antidepressant during late pregnancy could increase your risk of excessive bleeding after you give birth, and may cause serious medical complications in the baby. However, stopping the medicine may not be safe if you have a relapse of depression. Do not start or stop duloxetine without asking your doctor.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of duloxetine on the baby. Talk to your doctor about registering with the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants at 1-866-961-2388 or visit online at https://womensmentalhealth.org/research/pregnancyregistry/.
If you are breastfeeding, tell your doctor if you notice drowsiness, feeding problems, and slow weight gain in the nursing baby.

People with depression or mental illness may have thoughts about suicide. Some young people may have increased suicidal thoughts when first starting a medicine to treat depression. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Your family or caregivers should also watch for sudden changes in your behavior.
Taking an SNRI antidepressant during late pregnancy could increase your risk of excessive bleeding after you give birth, and may cause serious medical complications in the baby. However, stopping the medicine may not be safe if you have a relapse of depression. Do not start or stop duloxetine without asking your doctor.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of duloxetine on the baby. Talk to your doctor about registering with the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants at 1-866-961-2388 or visit online at https://womensmentalhealth.org/research/pregnancyregistry/.
If you are breastfeeding, tell your doctor if you notice drowsiness, feeding problems, and slow weight gain in the nursing baby.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Duloxetine is a selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressant (SSNRI). Duloxetine affects chemicals in the brain that may be unbalanced in people with depression.
Duloxetine is used to treat major depressive disorder in adults. It is also used to treat general anxiety disorder in adults and children who are at least 7 years old.
Duloxetine is also used in adults to treat nerve pain caused by diabetes (diabetic neuropathy), or chronic muscle or joint pain (such as low back pain and osteoarthritis pain).
Some brands of duloxetine are also used to treat fibromyalgia (a chronic pain disorder). Drizalma is for treating fibromyalgia only in adults. Cymbalta may be used to treat fibromyalgia in adults and children at least 13 years old.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
People with depression or mental illness may have thoughts about suicide. Some young people may have increased suicidal thoughts when first starting a medicine to treat depression. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Your family or caregivers should also watch for sudden changes in your behavior.
Taking an SNRI antidepressant during late pregnancy could increase your risk of excessive bleeding after you give birth, and may cause serious medical complications in the baby. However, stopping the medicine may not be safe if you have a relapse of depression. Do not start or stop duloxetine without asking your doctor.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of duloxetine on the baby. Talk to your doctor about registering with the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants at 1-866-961-2388 or visit online at https://womensmentalhealth.org/research/pregnancyregistry/.
If you are breastfeeding, tell your doctor if you notice drowsiness, feeding problems, and slow weight gain in the nursing baby.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries the warning specified by the object entity regarding use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
People with depression or mental illness may have thoughts about suicide. Some young people may have increased suicidal thoughts when first starting a medicine to treat depression. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Your family or caregivers should also watch for sudden changes in your behavior.
Taking an SNRI antidepressant during late pregnancy could increase your risk of excessive bleeding after you give birth, and may cause serious medical complications in the baby. However, stopping the medicine may not be safe if you have a relapse of depression. Do not start or stop duloxetine without asking your doctor.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of duloxetine on the baby. Talk to your doctor about registering with the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants at 1-866-961-2388 or visit online at https://womensmentalhealth.org/research/pregnancyregistry/.
If you are breastfeeding, tell your doctor if you notice drowsiness, feeding problems, and slow weight gain in the nursing baby.

graph_edge.subject: Prednisone
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject entity is a specific type or subtype of the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders. Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies, asthma and COPD flare-ups, rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands. Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones. Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).
Prednisone belongs to the drug class called glucocorticoids, which are a type of corticosteroid.

candidate_edges.subject: Prednisone
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject entity is a specific type or subtype of the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may decrease the effectiveness or response to the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Do not take prednisone if you have a systemic fungal infection, which is a fungal infection that has spread through your body.
Prednisone weakens your immune system. This makes it easier to get an infection; an existing infection may become worse and can reactivate an old infection, such as tuberculosis or hepatitis B. It can also hide the usual signs of infection, so an infection may be advanced before you notice it. Tell your doctor about any illness or infection you have had in the past few weeks.
Stay away from people who are sick. Chickenpox and measles can be serious or even fatal in someone taking a steroid. Call your doctor straight away if you are exposed to either one.
Do not have a live vaccine while you are taking prednisone unless your doctor says it is safe.
Do not stop taking prednisone suddenly after more than a few days of treatment. Your body needs time to start making its own steroid hormones again. Your doctor will lower your dose in steps.

candidate_edges.subject: Prednisone
candidate_edges.object: decrease maintenance dose after condition flares or serious illness
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

- Prednisone 1 mg tablets
- Prednisone 2.5 mg tablets

candidate_edges.object: doctor decides starting dose and lowers it in small steps
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.

Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders. Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies, asthma and COPD flare-ups, rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands. Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones. Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).
Prednisone belongs to the drug class called glucocorticoids, which are a type of corticosteroid.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.

The most common prednisone side effects are trouble sleeping, mood changes, increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention and swelling, increased sweating, acne, thinning skin that bruises easily, slow wound healing, higher blood sugar, indigestion and stomach upset.
Many of these effects are dose related. They are more likely on higher doses and on longer courses, and most settle after the medicine is stopped.
Serious prednisone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to prednisone: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
