candidate_edges.subject: Prednisone
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to decrease or lessen the condition or symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.

Prednisone side effects in women:
Women taking prednisone may notice irregular or missed periods, unwanted facial hair growth, acne and changes in body fat, such as a rounder face and more fat around the neck and waist. Long courses of prednisone also raise the risk of osteoporosis (thinning of the bones), and postmenopausal women are already at higher risk. Ask your doctor whether you need a bone density scan or a calcium and vitamin D supplement.
Long-term prednisone side effects:
Taking prednisone for months or years raises the risk of osteoporosis and broken bones, muscle weakness and muscle loss, cataracts and glaucoma, diabetes, high blood pressure, Cushing's syndrome (a set of changes caused by too much steroid, including a rounded face and fat around the trunk), and adrenal suppression, where your body stops making enough of its own steroid hormones.

Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders. Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies, asthma and COPD flare-ups, rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands. Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones. Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).

Common prednisone side effects:
The most common prednisone side effects are trouble sleeping, mood changes, increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention and swelling, increased sweating, acne, thinning skin that bruises easily, slow wound healing, higher blood sugar, indigestion and stomach upset.
Many of these effects are dose related. They are more likely on higher doses and on longer courses, and most settle after the medicine is stopped.
Serious prednisone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to prednisone: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of infection, such as fever, chills, sore throat, cough or a wound that is not healing, since prednisone can hide the usual warning signs;
- blurred vision, eye pain or seeing halos around lights, which can be signs of glaucoma (raised pressure in the eye) or cataracts;

There is no official cutoff, but doctors generally treat doses under 7.5 mg a day as low, 7.5 mg to 40 mg a day as moderate, and more than 40 mg a day as high. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:

Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.

The effect lasts longer than the drug itself. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
- Avoid being near people who are sick or have an infection. Call your doctor if you are exposed to chickenpox or measles.
- Do not have a live vaccine, such as MMR, chickenpox, rotavirus, yellow fever, oral typhoid, or the nasal flu vaccine, without your doctor's approval. Avoid close contact with someone who has just had an oral or nasal live vaccine.
- Limit alcohol. Both alcohol and prednisone irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach bleeding.
- Be careful with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin, since taking them with prednisone raises the risk of stomach bleeding.
- Your doctor may ask you to cut back on salt, since prednisone makes your body hold onto fluid.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Common prednisone side effects:
The most common prednisone side effects are trouble sleeping, mood changes, increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention and swelling, increased sweating, acne, thinning skin that bruises easily, slow wound healing, higher blood sugar, indigestion and stomach upset.
Many of these effects are dose related. They are more likely on higher doses and on longer courses, and most settle after the medicine is stopped.
Serious prednisone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to prednisone: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of infection, such as fever, chills, sore throat, cough or a wound that is not healing, since prednisone can hide the usual warning signs;
- blurred vision, eye pain or seeing halos around lights, which can be signs of glaucoma (raised pressure in the eye) or cataracts;

Do not take prednisone if you have a systemic fungal infection, which is a fungal infection that has spread through your body.
Prednisone weakens your immune system. This makes it easier to get an infection; an existing infection may become worse and can reactivate an old infection, such as tuberculosis or hepatitis B. It can also hide the usual signs of infection, so an infection may be advanced before you notice it. Tell your doctor about any illness or infection you have had in the past few weeks.
Stay away from people who are sick. Chickenpox and measles can be serious or even fatal in someone taking a steroid. Call your doctor straight away if you are exposed to either one.
Do not have a live vaccine while you are taking prednisone unless your doctor says it is safe.
Do not stop taking prednisone suddenly after more than a few days of treatment. Your body needs time to start making its own steroid hormones again. Your doctor will lower your dose in steps.

Prednisone side effects in women:
Women taking prednisone may notice irregular or missed periods, unwanted facial hair growth, acne and changes in body fat, such as a rounder face and more fat around the neck and waist. Long courses of prednisone also raise the risk of osteoporosis (thinning of the bones), and postmenopausal women are already at higher risk. Ask your doctor whether you need a bone density scan or a calcium and vitamin D supplement.
Long-term prednisone side effects:
Taking prednisone for months or years raises the risk of osteoporosis and broken bones, muscle weakness and muscle loss, cataracts and glaucoma, diabetes, high blood pressure, Cushing's syndrome (a set of changes caused by too much steroid, including a rounded face and fat around the trunk), and adrenal suppression, where your body stops making enough of its own steroid hormones.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone. It happens for two reasons. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks, and it increases appetite, which adds body fat over longer courses. It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist. Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop, but weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.
Can you drink alcohol while taking prednisone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and prednisone, but drinking is best kept to a minimum. Both irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. Alcohol also raises blood sugar and weakens bones, and prednisone does both of these too. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for you, especially if you are on a long course.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Long-term steroid use can cause bone loss. Your risk is higher if you smoke, if you do not exercise, if you do not get enough calcium or vitamin D, or if osteoporosis runs in your family. Talk with your doctor about protecting your bones.
Pregnancy:
Prednisone crosses the placenta. Taking it in the first trimester may raise the risk of birth defects, and taking higher doses later in pregnancy may affect the baby's growth and their adrenal glands. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Some conditions still need steroid treatment during pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than stopping on your own.
Breastfeeding:
Prednisone passes into breast milk in small amounts. Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding so you can talk through the dose and the timing of feeds.
Children:
Prednisone is used in children, but long courses can slow growth and affect bone development. The dose should not be higher than prescribed, and your child should be monitored during treatment.

- a seizure;

- headache;
- dizziness; or
- constipation or diarrhea.

graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Famotidine is a histamine-2 blocker that works by decreasing the amount of acid the stomach produces.
Famotidine is used to treat and prevent ulcers in the stomach and intestines. It also treats conditions in which the stomach produces too much acid, such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
Famotidine also treats gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and other conditions in which acid backs up from the stomach into the esophagus, causing heartburn.
The Zantac 360 brand of this medicine does not contain ranitidine, a medicine that was withdrawn from market in the United States.

- headache;

Get emergency medical help if you have any signs of an allergic reaction to famotidine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
- confusion, hallucinations, agitation, lack of energy;
- a seizure;
- fast or pounding heartbeats, sudden dizziness (like you might pass out).
Some side effects may be more likely in older adults and in people who have severe kidney disease.
Common famotidine side effects may include:
- headache;
- dizziness; or
- constipation or diarrhea.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: buspirone
candidate_edges.object: may be taken with or without food
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take buspirone exactly as it was prescribed for you. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose to make sure you get the best results. Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.
You may take buspirone with or without food but take it the same way each time.
Some buspirone tablets are scored so you can break the tablet into 2 or 3 pieces in order to take a smaller amount of the medicine at each dose. Do not use a tablet if it has not been broken correctly and the piece is too big or too small. Follow your doctor's instructions about how much of the tablet to take.
If you have difficulty swallowing capsules, you may open the capsule and sprinkle the medicine into a small amount (about 1 to 2 tablespoons) of applesauce. Swallow the mixture right away without chewing.

graph_edge.subject: Venlafaxine
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Venlafaxine is used in adults to treat major depressive disorder. Venlafaxine extended-release (long-acting) capsules are also used to treat generalized anxiety disorder (GAD; excessive worrying that is difficult to control), social anxiety disorder (extreme fear of interacting with others or performing in front of others that interferes with normal life), and panic disorder (sudden, unexpected attacks of extreme fear and worry about these attacks).
Venlafaxine belongs to a class of medications called selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). Venlafaxine works by increasing the amounts of serotonin and norepinephrine, natural substances in the brain that help maintain mental balance.

Take venlafaxine as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take with food at the same time each day.
Swallow the extended-release capsule or tablet whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
If you cannot swallow a capsule whole, open it and mix the medicine with applesauce. Swallow the mixture right away without chewing.
Tell your doctor if you have any changes in sexual function, such as loss of interest in sex, trouble having an orgasm, or (in men) problems with erections or ejaculation. Some sexual problems can be treated.
Your symptoms may not improve for up to several weeks. Do not stop using venlafaxine suddenly, or you could have severe and long-lasting unpleasant symptoms (such as agitation, confusion, tingling or electric shock feelings, aggression, violent behavior, suicidal thoughts, vision changes, or increased blood pressure). Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine.

Take venlafaxine as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take with food at the same time each day.
Swallow the extended-release capsule or tablet whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
If you cannot swallow a capsule whole, open it and mix the medicine with applesauce. Swallow the mixture right away without chewing.
Tell your doctor if you have any changes in sexual function, such as loss of interest in sex, trouble having an orgasm, or (in men) problems with erections or ejaculation. Some sexual problems can be treated.
Your symptoms may not improve for up to several weeks. Do not stop using venlafaxine suddenly, or you could have severe and long-lasting unpleasant symptoms (such as agitation, confusion, tingling or electric shock feelings, aggression, violent behavior, suicidal thoughts, vision changes, or increased blood pressure). Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take venlafaxine if you have uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma.
Do not use venlafaxine within 7 days before or 14 days after you have used an MAO inhibitor, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, or tranylcypromine.
Some young people have thoughts about suicide when first taking an antidepressant. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor, such as: mood or behavioral changes, anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, hyperactive (mentally or physically), more depressed, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself.
Do not stop using venlafaxine without first talking to your doctor.
Do not give this medicine to anyone younger than 18 years old without the advice of a doctor. Venlafaxine is not FDA approved for use in children.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries the warning specified by the object entity regarding use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Some young people may have increased suicidal thoughts when first starting a medicine to treat depression. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Your family or caregivers should also watch for sudden changes in your behavior.
Taking this medicine during pregnancy could harm the baby, and taking it in the month before delivery may increase your risk of severe bleeding after childbirth. However, stopping the medicine may not be safe for you. Do not start or stop venlafaxine without asking your doctor.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of venlafaxine on the baby.
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.subject: Venlafaxine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take venlafaxine as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take with food at the same time each day.
Swallow the extended-release capsule or tablet whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
If you cannot swallow a capsule whole, open it and mix the medicine with applesauce. Swallow the mixture right away without chewing.
Tell your doctor if you have any changes in sexual function, such as loss of interest in sex, trouble having an orgasm, or (in men) problems with erections or ejaculation. Some sexual problems can be treated.
Your symptoms may not improve for up to several weeks. Do not stop using venlafaxine suddenly, or you could have severe and long-lasting unpleasant symptoms (such as agitation, confusion, tingling or electric shock feelings, aggression, violent behavior, suicidal thoughts, vision changes, or increased blood pressure). Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine.

Take with food at the same time each day.
Swallow the extended-release capsule or tablet whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
If you cannot swallow a capsule whole, open it and mix the medicine with applesauce. Swallow the mixture right away without chewing.

graph_edge.subject: tramadol
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is a member of the pharmacological or therapeutic drug class specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Tramadol is an opioid agonist that may be used to treat moderate to moderately severe chronic pain in adults, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
- Extended-release forms of tramadol may be used in adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their pain for an extended period.
- An opioid pain medicine such as tramadol can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death.
Brands of tramadol include ConZip, Qdolo, Ryzolt, Ultram, Ultram ER, and Ultracet. Many have been discontinued, but generic tramadol is still available.
Taking tramadol in combination with other pain-relieving medicines such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin can provide better pain relief than just taking one pain-relieving medicine by itself (see Can you take tramadol in combination with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin?)

Dosage in kidney or liver impairment
- Severe kidney impairment: for immediate-release tramadol, doses are spaced 12 hours apart, and the maximum is 200 mg a day (four 50 mg tablets, given as two 100 mg doses 12 hours apart).

- Extended-release tramadol is not recommended for people with severe kidney or severe liver impairment.
Dosage in older adults
- No separate maximum dose applies on the basis of age, but tramadol should be started at the low end of the dosing range and increased slowly, with frequent review for drowsiness and breathing problems.

Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition. They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment.
Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS).
Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6. Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose. Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Tramadol should not be given to a child younger than 12 years old, or to anyone younger than 18 years old who has recently had surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Extended-release tramadol should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines. Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, and medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body. Because starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance, tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol. Tell your doctor if you also use:
- medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
- other opioid medicines
- buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine. These opioids work differently and can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms, so they are generally not taken with tramadol
- a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax

candidate_edges.subject: tramadol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug has a drug interaction with the drug or substance specified by the object entity that may change effects or cause harm.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency help or call 911 right away if you take too many tramadol (overdose). When you first start taking tramadol, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur. Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose.
Taking tramadol with other opioid medicines, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids (gabapentin or pregabalin), alcohol, or other central nervous system depressants (including street drugs) can cause severe drowsiness, decreased awareness, breathing problems, coma, and death.
Do not take tramadol with any other medicine that contains tramadol. Check the label of every pain medicine you take, as some combination products contain tramadol.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tramadol is used for the management of moderate to moderately severe pain in adults, including postoperative pain (pain after surgery).
Tramadol treats pain severe enough to require opioids and may be used as an alternative to other forms of pain relief that did not relieve pain well enough or were not tolerated.
Tramadol extended-release capsules may be used by adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their moderate to moderately severe chronic pain for an extended time.
Tramadol should not be used in children younger than 12 years old, or anyone younger than 18 years old with other risk factors (such as breathing problems), or who have recently had surgery to remove their tonsils or adenoids.
- Extended-release tramadol (Ultram ER) should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.

You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines. - headache

Serious tramadol side effects and warnings:
Tramadol may cause serious side effects, some of which may be fatal.
Tramadol can slow or stop your breathing and may be habit-forming. MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription. Keep this medicine where others cannot get to it. Do not take more tramadol than prescribed, as an overdose can be fatal. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.

Tramadol may cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive or perform hazardous tasks. Do not perform these tasks if tramadol causes confusion, mental impairment, or drowsiness.
Tramadol can cause withdrawal symptom s if stopped suddenly after being taken for a long period of time. Symptoms may include restlessness, drug craving, anxiety, and sweating. This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take tramadol if you are:
- are allergic to tramadol, to any of the other ingredients in your product, or to other opioids
- have significant breathing problems (respiratory depression)
- have acute or severe asthma and are somewhere you cannot be monitored, or where resuscitation equipment is not available
- have a known or suspected blockage of the stomach or intestines, including paralytic ileus

- are younger than 12 years of age
- are younger than 18 years of age and have recently had surgery to remove your tonsils or adenoids.
Seizures have occurred in some people taking tramadol. Your seizure risk may be higher if you have ever had:
- a head injury, epilepsy, or other seizure disorder
- drug or alcohol addiction or
- a metabolic disorder.
To make sure tramadol is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have a history of:
- Head injury or seizures
- Problems urinating
- Liver, kidney, or thyroid problems

- gas, stomach pain; or
- the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug may need the medical test or monitoring specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia), or if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition, your blood may need to be tested often. Your heart rate may also be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG) to measure electrical activity of the heart. This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness or limp feeling, severe stomach pain, and numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor. If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.object: call your doctor for medical advice about side effects
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
- severe throat irritation;
- stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
- high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
- signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
- gas, stomach pain; or
- the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
- severe throat irritation;
- stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
- high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
- signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
- gas, stomach pain; or
- the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should not be used by patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia), or if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition, your blood may need to be tested often. Your heart rate may also be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG) to measure electrical activity of the heart. This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness or limp feeling, severe stomach pain, and numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor. If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.

Mix the powder form of this medicine with at least 4 ounces (one-half cup) of cold water or fruit juice before taking. Drink the mixture slowly, over 5 to 10 minutes in all. To make sure you get the entire dose, add a little more water to the same glass, swirl gently and drink right away.
To be sure this medicine is helping your condition, you may need frequent blood tests. You may not notice any change in your symptoms, but your blood work will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium chloride. Your heart function may need to be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG). Even if you have no symptoms, tests can help your doctor determine if this medicine is effective.
Your treatment may include a special diet. Follow the diet plan created for you by your doctor or nutrition counselor. Get familiar with the list of foods you should eat or avoid to help control your condition.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take potassium chloride exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or with a special dose-measuring spoon or medicine cup. If you do not have a dose-measuring device, ask your pharmacist for one.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on a tablet or capsule. Sucking on the pill could irritate your mouth or throat.
Call your doctor if you have trouble swallowing a potassium chloride capsule or tablet. You may be able to dissolve the tablet in water, or mix the medicine from a capsule with soft food. Carefully follow your doctor's instructions.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia), or if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition, your blood may need to be tested often. Your heart rate may also be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG) to measure electrical activity of the heart. This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness or limp feeling, severe stomach pain, and numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor. If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.

candidate_edges.subject: Potassium Chloride
candidate_edges.object: call your doctor for medical advice about side effects
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
- severe throat irritation;
- stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
- high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
- signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
- gas, stomach pain; or
- the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain, below the outer layer known as the cortex. It is not a cortical depressant, meaning it does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain the way some other sedatives do.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. This is what relieves itching.

Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting. This is an approved use for the injection, but not for the forms taken by mouth.

In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.

In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.

Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine. Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses, the same doses, the same warnings, and the same side effects.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine. Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses, the same doses, the same warnings, and the same side effects.
The injection is the exception. It is a hydroxyzine HCl product; there is no pamoate injection, and it has its own approved uses, doses, and warnings.
The practical differences are:
- Form. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution. Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.
- How they dissolve. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride is very soluble in water. Hydroxyzine pamoate is practically insoluble in water.
- How the strength is measured. Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by the amount of hydroxyzine HCl they are equivalent to. A 25 mg pamoate capsule delivers the same amount of active medicine as a hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg tablet.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is given through the route of administration specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses. These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
- Anxiety and tension. For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
- Itching from allergic skin conditions. For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant. It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
- Sedation around surgery. As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings. It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety. Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months. Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug should avoid the substance or activity specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses. These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
- Anxiety and tension. For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
- Itching from allergic skin conditions. For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant. It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
- Sedation around surgery. As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings. It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety. Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months. Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain, below the outer layer known as the cortex. It is not a cortical depressant, meaning it does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain the way some other sedatives do.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle, widens the airways (bronchodilation), and reduces pain. These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.
Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting. This is an approved use for the injection, but not for the forms taken by mouth.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may cause the adverse effect or symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine
candidate_edges.relation_definition: In case of an overdose of the subject drug the patient should follow the instruction specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
The most common sign of hydroxyzine overdose is heavy sedation. Other reported signs include seizures (convulsions), stupor, nausea, and vomiting.
Overdose can also cause QT prolongation and Torsade de Pointes, so heart monitoring with an ECG is recommended.
There is no specific antidote for hydroxyzine overdose.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine
candidate_edges.object: tell doctor if you have family history of long QT syndrome
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tell your doctor if you have anything that raises your risk of a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation. This includes:
- congenital long QT syndrome, a heart rhythm condition you are born with
- a family history of long QT syndrome
- a recent heart attack
- heart failure that is not well controlled
- a slow or irregular heartbeat (bradyarrhythmia)
- other conditions that make heart rhythm problems more likely
Hydroxyzine should not be given to women who are breastfeeding. It is not known whether hydroxyzine passes into breast milk, but many medicines do.
The oral solution contains a small amount of alcohol, 0.5% by volume, and is sweetened with sucrose. Tell your doctor if either of these matters for you.

Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections. This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill. Your blood may need to be tested often. Visit your doctor regularly.

Stop taking this medicine and call your doctor right away if you have painful urination, blood in your urine, burning in your eyes, swelling in your face or throat, skin redness or a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use this medicine if you have ever had an allergic reaction to allopurinol.
Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections. This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill. Your blood may need to be tested often. Visit your doctor regularly.
In rare cases, allopurinol may cause a severe allergic reaction. Stop taking this medicine and call your doctor right away if you have painful urination, blood in your urine, burning in your eyes, swelling in your face or throat, skin redness or a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling.
Avoid drinking alcohol. It can make your condition worse. Allopurinol may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug may need the medical test or monitoring specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use this medicine if you have ever had an allergic reaction to allopurinol.
Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections. This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill. Your blood may need to be tested often. Visit your doctor regularly.
In rare cases, allopurinol may cause a severe allergic reaction. Stop taking this medicine and call your doctor right away if you have painful urination, blood in your urine, burning in your eyes, swelling in your face or throat, skin redness or a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling.
Avoid drinking alcohol. It can make your condition worse. Allopurinol may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug may need the medical test or monitoring specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take allopurinol exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take the tablets with a full glass of water. To reduce your risk of kidney stones, drink 8 to 10 full glasses of fluid every day, unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
Take allopurinol tablets after meals to help prevent stomach upset.
Allopurinol injection is injected into a vein by a healthcare provider. The injection is usually only used if you are unable to take medicine by mouth.
You may need frequent medical tests while using this medicine, even if you have no symptoms.
Your kidney and liver function may also need to be tested. Your doctor may change your dose if your kidney function changes.
You may have gout attacks when you first start taking allopurinol tablets. Your doctor may recommend another gout medication to take with allopurinol. Keep taking the medicine as directed.

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Use these medicines exactly as directed.
Clopidogrel can be taken with or without food.
Clopidogrel is sometimes taken together with aspirin. Take aspirin only if your doctor tells you to.
Clopidogrel keeps your blood from coagulating (clotting) and can make it easier for you to bleed, even from a minor injury. Contact your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have any bleeding that will not stop.
You may need to stop using clopidogrel for a short time before a surgery, medical procedure, or dental work. Any healthcare provider who treats you should know that you are taking clopidogrel.
Do not stop taking clopidogrel without first talking to your doctor, even if you have signs of bleeding. Stopping the medicine could increase your risk of a heart attack or stroke.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
- any active bleeding; or
- a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain (such as from a head injury).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- an ulcer in your stomach or intestines; or
- a bleeding disorder or blood clotting disorder.
Clopidogrel may not work as well if you have certain genetic factors that affect the breakdown of this medicine in your body. Your doctor may perform a blood test to make sure clopidogrel is right for you.
This medicine is not expected to harm an unborn baby. However, taking clopidogrel within 1 week before childbirth can cause bleeding in the mother. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
You should not breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
- any active bleeding; or
- a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain (such as from a head injury).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- an ulcer in your stomach or intestines; or
- a bleeding disorder or blood clotting disorder.
Clopidogrel may not work as well if you have certain genetic factors that affect the breakdown of this medicine in your body. Your doctor may perform a blood test to make sure clopidogrel is right for you.
This medicine is not expected to harm an unborn baby. However, taking clopidogrel within 1 week before childbirth can cause bleeding in the mother. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
You should not breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.subject: clopidogrel
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used together with the other treatment or lifestyle measure specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Use these medicines exactly as directed.
Clopidogrel can be taken with or without food.
Clopidogrel is sometimes taken together with aspirin. Take aspirin only if your doctor tells you to.
Clopidogrel keeps your blood from coagulating (clotting) and can make it easier for you to bleed, even from a minor injury. Contact your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have any bleeding that will not stop.
You may need to stop using clopidogrel for a short time before a surgery, medical procedure, or dental work. Any healthcare provider who treats you should know that you are taking clopidogrel.
Do not stop taking clopidogrel without first talking to your doctor, even if you have signs of bleeding. Stopping the medicine could increase your risk of a heart attack or stroke.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: Patients taking the subject drug may need the medical test or monitoring specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
- any active bleeding; or
- a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain (such as from a head injury).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- an ulcer in your stomach or intestines; or
- a bleeding disorder or blood clotting disorder.
Clopidogrel may not work as well if you have certain genetic factors that affect the breakdown of this medicine in your body. Your doctor may perform a blood test to make sure clopidogrel is right for you.
This medicine is not expected to harm an unborn baby. However, taking clopidogrel within 1 week before childbirth can cause bleeding in the mother. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
You should not breastfeed while using this medicine.

candidate_edges.subject: Ergocalciferol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
- high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
- high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
- any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease;
- kidney disease; or
- an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about, such as peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes. Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby, and your dose needs may be different during pregnancy. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk and may cause side effects in the nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice. Your child's dose will depend on age, weight, diet, and other factors.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop taking ergocalciferol and call your doctor at once if you have:
- chest pain, feeling short of breath;
- growth problems (in a child taking ergocalciferol); or
- early signs of vitamin D overdose --weakness, metallic taste in your mouth, weight loss, muscle or bone pain, constipation, nausea, and vomiting.
Less serious side effects may be more likely, and you may have none at all.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.subject: Ergocalciferol
candidate_edges.object: ask a doctor before using if you have allergies
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
- high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
- high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
- any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease;
- kidney disease; or
- an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about, such as peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes. Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby, and your dose needs may be different during pregnancy. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk and may cause side effects in the nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice. Your child's dose will depend on age, weight, diet, and other factors.

candidate_edges.subject: Ergocalciferol
candidate_edges.object: inform doctor about all other medicines
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Certain medications can make it harder for your body to absorb vitamin D. If you take other medications, take them at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after you take ergocalciferol.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines, especially:
- a diuretic or "water pill"; or
- mineral oil (sometimes taken as a laxative).
This list is not complete. Other drugs may affect ergocalciferol, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible drug interactions are listed here.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Ergocalciferol is vitamin D2. Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium.
Ergocalciferol is used to treat hypoparathyroidism (decreased functioning of the parathyroid glands).
Ergocalciferol is also used to treat rickets (softening of the bones caused by vitamin D deficiency) or low levels of phosphate in the blood (hypophosphatemia).
Ergocalciferol may also be used for purposes not listed in this medication guide.

Less serious side effects may be more likely, and you may have none at all.

candidate_edges.subject: Ergocalciferol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug necessitates changes or modifications to the treatment or dosage specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
- high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
- high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
- any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease;
- kidney disease; or
- an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about, such as peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes. Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby, and your dose needs may be different during pregnancy. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk and may cause side effects in the nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice. Your child's dose will depend on age, weight, diet, and other factors.

candidate_edges.subject: Ergocalciferol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
- high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
- high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
- any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease;
- kidney disease; or
- an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about, such as peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes. Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby, and your dose needs may be different during pregnancy. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk and may cause side effects in the nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice. Your child's dose will depend on age, weight, diet, and other factors.

If you are taking cetirizine for hives, get emergency medical help immediately if you have trouble swallowing, dizziness, swelling of the tongue or around the mouth, trouble speaking, drooling, or wheezing. Cetirizine is not a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Do not use cetirizine to prevent hives from known causes such as foods, insect stings, or medicines. Call your doctor if your hives do not improve after 3 days, if they last more than 6 weeks, or if they are an unusual color, look bruised or blistered, or do not itch.
Rarely, some people have reported severe itching when stopping cetirizine after daily, long-term use of at least a few months or several years. If you experience widespread, severe itching on stopping this medication, contact your healthcare provider.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Cetirizine is a second generation antihistamine that reduces the natural chemical histamine in the body. Histamine can produce symptoms of sneezing, itching, watery eyes, and runny nose.
Cetirizine is used to treat cold or allergy symptoms such as sneezing, itching, watery eyes, or runny nose.
Cetirizine is also used to treat an allergic reaction, itching and swelling caused by chronic urticaria (hives) and minimizes or eliminates the symptoms of perennial allergic rhinitis, seasonal allergic rhinitis, chronic idiopathic urticaria, allergic asthma, physical urticaria, and atopic dermatitis.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
If you are taking cetirizine for hives, get emergency medical help immediately if you have trouble swallowing, dizziness, swelling of the tongue or around the mouth, trouble speaking, drooling, or wheezing. Cetirizine is not a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Do not use cetirizine to prevent hives from known causes such as foods, insect stings, or medicines. Call your doctor if your hives do not improve after 3 days, if they last more than 6 weeks, or if they are an unusual color, look bruised or blistered, or do not itch.
Rarely, some people have reported severe itching when stopping cetirizine after daily, long-term use of at least a few months or several years. If you experience widespread, severe itching on stopping this medication, contact your healthcare provider.

If you are taking cetirizine for hives, get emergency medical help immediately if you have trouble swallowing, dizziness, swelling of the tongue or around the mouth, trouble speaking, drooling, or wheezing. Cetirizine is not a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Do not use cetirizine to prevent hives from known causes such as foods, insect stings, or medicines. Call your doctor if your hives do not improve after 3 days, if they last more than 6 weeks, or if they are an unusual color, look bruised or blistered, or do not itch.
Rarely, some people have reported severe itching when stopping cetirizine after daily, long-term use of at least a few months or several years. If you experience widespread, severe itching on stopping this medication, contact your healthcare provider.

Ondansetron can cause a serious heart problem, especially if you use certain medicines at the same time, including antibiotics, antidepressants, heart rhythm medicine, antipsychotic medicines, and medicines to treat cancer, malaria, HIV or AIDS. Tell your doctor about all medicines you use, and those you start or stop using during your treatment with ondansetron.
Taking ondansetron while you are using certain other medicines can cause high levels of serotonin to build up in your body, a condition called "serotonin syndrome," which can be fatal. Tell your doctor if you also use:
- medicine to treat depression;
- medicine to treat a psychiatric disorder;
- a narcotic (opioid) medication; or
- medicine to prevent nausea and vomiting.
This list is not complete and many other drugs can interact with ondansetron. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Ondansetron can cause a serious heart problem, especially if you use certain medicines at the same time, including antibiotics, antidepressants, heart rhythm medicine, antipsychotic medicines, and medicines to treat cancer, malaria, HIV or AIDS. Tell your doctor about all medicines you use, and those you start or stop using during your treatment with ondansetron.
Taking ondansetron while you are using certain other medicines can cause high levels of serotonin to build up in your body, a condition called "serotonin syndrome," which can be fatal. Tell your doctor if you also use:
- medicine to treat depression;
- medicine to treat a psychiatric disorder;
- a narcotic (opioid) medication; or
- medicine to prevent nausea and vomiting.
This list is not complete and many other drugs can interact with ondansetron. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
You should not use ondansetron if:
- you are also using apomorphine (Apokyn); or
- you are allergic to ondansetron or similar medicines (dolasetron, granisetron, palonosetron).
To make sure ondansetron is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have:
- liver disease;
- an electrolyte imbalance (such as low levels of potassium or magnesium in your blood);
- congestive heart failure, slow heartbeats;
- a personal or family history of long QT syndrome; or
- a blockage in your digestive tract (stomach or intestines).
Ondansetron is not expected to harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant.
It is not known whether ondansetron passes into breast milk or if it could harm a nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding a baby.
Ondansetron is not approved for use by anyone younger than 1 month old.
Ondansetron orally disintegrating tablets may contain phenylalanine. Tell your doctor if you have phenylketonuria (PKU).

Take ondansetron exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.
Ondansetron can be taken with or without food.
The first dose is usually taken before the start of your surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation treatment. Follow your doctor's dosing instructions very carefully.
Take the ondansetron regular tablet with a full glass of water.
To take the orally disintegrating tablet (Zofran ODT):
- Keep the tablet in its blister pack until you are ready to take it. Open the package and peel back the foil. Do not push a tablet through the foil or you may damage the tablet.
- Use dry hands to remove the tablet and place it in your mouth.
- Do not swallow the tablet whole. Allow it to dissolve in your mouth without chewing.
- Swallow several times as the tablet dissolves.
To use ondansetron oral soluble film (strip) (Zuplenz):
- Keep the strip in the foil pouch until you are ready to use the medicine.

reference_evidence:
Usual Adult Dose of Ondansetron for Nausea/Vomiting -- Chemotherapy Induced:
Oral: Highly Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (HEC): -Recommended dose: 24 mg orally 30 minutes before the start of single-day HEC (including cisplatin doses of 50 mg/m2 or greater) Moderately Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (MEC): -Recommended dose: 8 mg orally twice a day, with the first dose administered 30 minutes before the start of chemotherapy and the subsequent dose 8 hours later; then 8 mg orally 2 times a day (every 12 hours) for 1 to 2 days after the completion of chemotherapy Parenteral: -Recommended dose: 0.15 mg/kg IV, with the first dose (infused over 15 minutes) 30 minutes before the start of emetogenic chemotherapy and subsequent doses given 4 and 8 hours after the first dose. -Maximum dose: 16 mg per dose Comments: -Multi-day, single-dose administration of 24 mg orally for HEC has not been studied. -The injection formulation should be diluted prior to IV administration. Uses: -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with HEC or MEC -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with initial and repeat courses of emetogenic chemotherapy
